newsitem.title: GERMANY: German debt bounds higher amid friendly U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: German debt bounds higher amid friendly U.S. data.

text.p: German debt burst higher on Friday, setting several new record highs along the way, as the dour state of Germany's economy and news the U.S. economy was still growing without inflation sweetened the market's mood.

German Bund futures, following a recent days' pattern, got off to strong start in the morning as the contract reached its first new high at 103.54. The rise was largely attributed to the U.S. market's strong performance overnight amid relief at the end of the U.S. Treasury's quarterly refunding auction.
Also a 4.4 percent drop in German December retail sales helped buoy the market.
Having digested the morning's first record, the market stormed higher again in early afternoon as U.S. inflation data was friendlier than expected.

Jumping 15 ticks on news that the U.S. January producer price index fell 0.3 percent, registering its first drop since October 1994, the Bund futures contract roared to the 103.82 level. Economists had expected to see a 0.3 percent increase.
The gains left dealers virtually delirious, predicting the market could possibly even reach the 104 level today.
But profit-taking also emerged late in the session and took the DTB March Bund futures contract to 103.61.
Late in the day dealers said that investors were beginning to get slightly nervous, prompting some of the profit-taking seen this afternoon.
But overall the mood remains very buoyant as few expect a sharp turnaround in the German economy in the near term.

Investors still count on low German interest rates and possibly even another cut some time during the cycle. There is very little speculation however that the Bundesbank could take action at next week's council meeting.
Due to Monday's U.S. holiday, dealers predicted the markets would lack new direction, leaving them to trade in a range.
Dealers said that the range for Monday would likely be between 103.60 to 103.85.
